diagnostic_evidence.quote: Suppose $\omega_0,\ \omega_1$ are two $1$-homogeneous symplectic forms on $M$, for which $(\omega_0)_{|N} =(\omega_1)_{|N} $.

By the homogeneous Darboux-Weinstein Theorem (\ref{thm: Darboux-Weinstein}), there exists $\Psi:T^*P\rightarrow T^*P$ such that $\omega_{can} = \Psi^*\Omega$ and $(T^*h_z)^*\Psi = \Psi$ in a neighborhood of the zero section in $T^*P$.

issues.failure_explanation: The Moser argument needs the interpolation $\omega_s=(1-s)\omega_0+s\omega_1$ to be symplectic near $N$, but the stated hypothesis only says the two forms agree when restricted to $N$, which does not imply this. Counterexample inside the paper's setting: $M=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^\times$ with $h_z(q,t)=(q,zt)$, $\omega_0=dq\wedge dt$, $\omega_1=-dq\wedge dt$ (both symplectic and 1-homogeneous), $N=\{q=0\}$: both forms restrict to 0 on the 1-dimensional $N$, yet $\omega_{1/2}\equiv 0$ is degenerate on every neighborhood of $N$, so the field $\eta_s$ with $i_{\eta_s}\omega_s=\beta$ cannot be constructed and the proof collapses. Nondegeneracy along $N$ would follow from the stronger hypothesis $\omega_0(p)=\omega_1(p)$ as bilinear forms at points $p\in N$; under that reading, however, the paper's own application in Section 4.2 is no longer covered: at points of the zero section $\Omega=\int_0^1(\phi_X^s)^*\omega_{can}ds$ equals $\omega_{can}$ only on pairs tangent to the zero section and differs by the vertical term $\pi(\cdot_\xi,\cdot_\xi)$ (on vertical pairs $\omega_{can}=0$ but $\Omega=\pi$).

failure_location.quote: Since $\omega_s|_X$ is symplectic for all $s\in[0,1]$, this is true for a small neighborhood of $N$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either restate the theorem with pointwise agreement along $N$ (making the Moser proof valid) and supply the missing direct argument for the Section 4.2 instance (there the interpolation $\omega_{can}+s(\Omega-\omega_{can})$ is nondegenerate along the zero section because the extra term is purely vertical-vertical, so Moser applies after an explicit check), or keep the weak hypothesis and add a linear-algebra/Whitney-extension reduction to the pointwise case.
issues.overall_effect: Both statements of the homogeneous Darboux-Weinstein theorem (thm: Darboux-Weinstein and its appendix duplicate thm:added-1) are unproven as written; the construction of $\Psi$ converting the Weinstein realization into the Karasev realization in Section 4.2, and hence Proposition thm: bi-realization ('Any homogeneous Poisson spray induces a homogeneous bi-realization'), rest on this theorem applied with only restriction-agreement of the forms.
issues.title: Homogeneous Darboux-Weinstein proof assumes nondegeneracy of the interpolated forms without justification
issues.why_classification: The proof of a central tool and its key application fail, but a complete resolution exists without new global architecture: a hypothesis strengthening plus one contained nondegeneracy check (or one contained linear-algebra lemma), with all downstream results surviving.

issues.failure_explanation: The $q,p,z$ components of the displayed $\alpha$ follow the quoted Karasev expansion $\alpha^i=y^i+\frac{1}{2}\pi^{vi}\xi_v$ applied to the displayed $\Pi$ (components $\Pi^{p_iq^i}=1/t$, $\Pi^{zt}=+1$), but the $t$-component does not: the expansion gives $\alpha^t=t+\frac{1}{2}\xi_z$ (and $\beta^t=t-\frac{1}{2}\xi_z$ via $\beta(y,\xi)=\alpha(y,-\xi)$), whereas the paper writes $t-\frac{1}{2}\xi_z$ (and $t+\frac{1}{2}\xi_z$). As written, $\alpha$ is not a Poisson map: in the $(z,t)$-sector the Poisson-map condition gives $\pi_{can}(\alpha^*\lambda,\alpha^*\mu)=0$ while $\Pi(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda_z\mu_t-\lambda_t\mu_z\neq 0$. Under the opposite global sign convention the $q,p,z$ components would all be wrong instead; under any single convention the displayed pair fails to be a bi-realization of the stated $\Pi$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Flip the sign of the $\xi_z$-correction in the $t$-components: $\alpha^t=t+\frac{1}{2}\xi_z$, $\beta^t=t-\frac{1}{2}\xi_z$; the remaining components, the homogeneity analysis and the order-2 claim are then consistent.
issues.overall_effect: The explicit order-2 approximation of the Karasev bi-realization for the canonical contact structure (both displayed formulas, eq: bi-realization example and eq: bi-realization example2) is incorrect: $\alpha$ as displayed is not a Poisson map and $\beta$ not anti-Poisson for the stated $\Pi$. No other labelled result uses these formulas.
issues.title: Sign error in the t-components of the explicit order-2 bi-realization of the contact example
issues.why_classification: A forced local sign correction in one component of each displayed formula restores the stated Poisson/anti-Poisson properties; no other claim or guarantee is affected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: in that case we call variation functions to any time-dependent functions $(f_s)_{s\in I}$ such that $df_s = \xi_s$, for all $s\in I$.

issues.failure_explanation: Variation functions are defined only up to additive constants, and 1-homogeneity of $\xi_s=df_s$ only forces $h_z^*f_s-zf_s$ to be constant on each component, not zero. Counterexample: an exact family with $\xi_s\equiv 0$ (e.g. a constant family $L_s\equiv L$) admits the variation function $f_s\equiv 1$, which is 0-homogeneous, while $\xi_s=0$ is homogeneous of every degree; the 'only if' direction fails. The correct statement is that $\xi_s$ is 1-homogeneous iff $f_s$ can be chosen 1-homogeneous (the obstruction $c(z)=h_z^*f-zf$ satisfies $c(z)=k(1-z)$, so a constant shift works).

failure_location.quote: Then $\xi_s$ are $1$-homogeneous if and only if $f_s$ are $1$-homogeneous.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate as '$\xi_s$ is 1-homogeneous if and only if $f_s$ can be chosen 1-homogeneous (up to additive constants)'; constants do not affect Hamiltonian flows, so the intended use survives.
issues.overall_effect: The corollary, used to justify that the variation functions (the approximate Hamiltonians in the integrator construction) inherit homogeneity, is false as stated.
issues.title: Variation-function homogeneity corollary ignores additive constants
issues.why_classification: A local rewording ('can be chosen'/'up to constants') with a one-line adjustment argument preserves the corollary's role and all uses.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: since $\omega_{can} = dx\wedge d\xi_x + dt\wedge d\xi_t$ is 1-homogeneous
The family $L_s = \phi^s_H(L)$ is an exact smooth family of homogeneous Lagrangian submanifolds, and the variation form at $t$ is $dH$.

issues.failure_explanation: With the paper's $\omega_{can}=dq\wedge d\xi$ and the defining relation (eq: variation form), the variation form of the graph family $L_s=\mathrm{graph}(\zeta_s)$ is $-\tau^*\partial_s\zeta_s$, not $+\tau^*\partial_s\zeta_s$: for $\zeta_s=s\,dq$ the normal variation is $\partial_\xi$ and $\xi_{s_0}(\partial_q)=(dq\wedge d\xi)(\partial_\xi,\partial_q)=-1$, while $\tau^*\partial_s\zeta_s(\partial_q)=+1$. Cross-check: the same family is $L_s=\phi^s_{-q}(L_0)$, so by ex: dH the variation form is $d(-q)=-dq$, consistent with (eq: variation form) and inconsistent with the claimed formula. The same sign error appears in the first example of Section 5.2, where the claimed variation form $\Phi_H^{-t*}dH$ of the graphs $G^t_H$ should be its negative (direct computation with $\Omega=\pi_1^*\omega-\pi_2^*\omega$); that derivation also misapplies Proposition prop: two symplectic lagrangian, since the map $\Phi_H^{-t}$ there depends on the family parameter.

failure_location.quote: The homogeneous variation form at $t$ is $\tau^*\partial_s \zeta_s$, where $\tau$ is the cotangent projection.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Flip the sign ($\xi_s=-\tau^*\partial_s\zeta_s$, and correspondingly in Section 5.2), or equivalently change the convention in (eq: variation form) consistently throughout (which would then break ex: dH instead).
issues.overall_effect: The stated variation forms of the graph families in ex: cotangent projec and in Section 5.2 (hence also the formula '$\tau^*d\frac{\partial\mathbf{S}_t}{\partial t}$' for the Hamilton-Jacobi family) have the wrong sign relative to the paper's own definitions; exactness and homogeneity of the families are unaffected.
issues.title: Wrong sign for the variation form of graphs of 1-forms
issues.why_classification: Local sign corrections in two example computations; the families' defining properties (Lagrangian, homogeneous, exact) and all downstream constructions are unaffected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Moreover, given a bisection $L$, the inverse restricted to $L$, $\alpha^{-1}_{|L}$ is also homogeneous: $\alpha^{-1}_{|L}\circ h_z = T^*h_z\circ\alpha^{-1}_{|L}$.

issues.failure_explanation: The equivariance chain $\phi_L\circ h_z=h_z\circ\phi_L$ uses $\alpha^{-1}_{|L}\circ h_z$, which is only well defined if $h_z(\alpha(L))=\alpha(L)$, i.e. if the bisection $L$ is $\mathbb{R}^\times$-invariant; Lagrangian-ness does not imply invariance under the free principal action. A Lagrangian bisection obtained, for example, by perturbing the identity bisection with a non-1-homogeneous generating function is not invariant, and its induced diffeomorphism is then not homogeneous. Hence the homogeneity part of item (1), and the preceding remark that 'any bisection induces a homogeneous diffeomorphism', are false without the hypothesis that $L$ is homogeneous; only the Poisson part is the cited Coste-Dazord-Weinstein result.

failure_location.quote: the induced diffeomorphism $\phi_L:P_J\rightarrow P_J$ is a homogeneous Poisson diffeomorphism;

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add 'homogeneous' to the hypothesis on $L$ in prop:added-4 and in the preceding remark.
issues.overall_effect: prop:added-4(1) and the preceding remark overstate the homogeneity conclusion; Section 6's prose ('given a Lagrangian bisection $L$...') inherits the missing hypothesis, though the paper's actual constructions use homogeneous bisections.
issues.title: Lagrangian bisections claimed to induce homogeneous diffeomorphisms without invariance
issues.why_classification: Adding the standard hypothesis, which all bisections actually used in the paper satisfy, repairs the proposition and remark with no mathematical loss.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: A submanifold $L\subset \mathcal{G}$ is called a bisection if the restrictions of both source and target to $L$ are diffeomorphisms onto $M$.

issues.failure_explanation: The two projections of $T^*Q\times T^*Q$ restrict to diffeomorphisms of $\Psi^{-1}(\mathrm{graph}(d\mathbf{S}_t))$ onto $T^*Q$ only if the mixed Hessian $\partial^2\mathbf{S}_t/\partial q\partial\bar{q}$ is everywhere nondegenerate. For a general solution this fails: for $H\equiv 0$ any time-independent separable $\mathbf{S}=f(q)+g(\bar q)$ solves (eq: H-J) and has identically zero mixed Hessian; the second projection then has $n$-dimensional image and is not surjective onto the $2n$-dimensional $T^*Q$. The displayed set is Lagrangian (via $\Psi$ and prop: mu closed) but not a bisection.

failure_location.quote: For instance, for any solution $\mathbf{S}_t$ of (\ref{eq: H-J}), a smooth family of Lagrangian bisections of the pair groupoid is given by $\Psi^{-1}(\underline{d\mathbf{S}_t}) = \{(d_q\mathbf{S}_t(q,\bar{q}), -d_{\bar{q}}\mathbf{S}_t(q,\bar{q})),\ (q,\bar{q})\in Q\times Q\}\subset T^*Q\times T^*Q$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the claim to solutions whose mixed Hessian $\partial^2\mathbf{S}/\partial q\partial\bar q$ is nondegenerate (the standard generating-function condition).
issues.overall_effect: The claim that any Hamilton-Jacobi solution yields Lagrangian bisections of the pair groupoid (the bridge from the HJ equation to the integrator construction) is false as stated.
issues.title: HJ solutions claimed to give bisections without a nondegeneracy condition
issues.why_classification: A standard nondegeneracy hypothesis restores the claim; the construction for nondegenerate solutions is unaffected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Theorem \ref{thm: ham flow} guarantees that, given a Lagrangian bisection $L$, the induced diffeomorphism $\varphi_L$ is a Hamiltonian flow.
when $L \xhookrightarrow{} (\Sigma,\omega)$ is a Lagrangian bisection for $R$, the induced map $\varphi_L = \beta\circ \alpha^{-1}_{|L}$ defines a Poisson diffeomorphism $(P,\Pi)\rightarrow (P,\Pi)$.
This grants the existence of JHI's, constructed as explained above.

issues.failure_explanation: The paper's central constructive claim — that approximating the variation functions to order $k$ makes the bisection-induced diffeomorphisms satisfy the hPHI definition (each $\phi_\epsilon$ exactly the time-$\epsilon$ flow of a homogeneous $\mathcal{H}_s=H^P+o(s^{k-1})$) — is asserted with no argument. The cited Theorem thm: ham flow only guarantees that $\varphi_L$ is a Poisson diffeomorphism (its item 1); the exact-flow property (item 3) holds only for the exact family $L_s=\phi^s_{\alpha^*H}(\sigma(P))$, and the invoking sentence misstates the theorem as '$\varphi_L$ is a Hamiltonian flow'. Verifying the definition requires a missing nontrivial argument: the near-identity family from the approximate bisections must be shown to be generated by locally Hamiltonian, 0-homogeneous fields with 1-homogeneous primitives (unique only up to constants) matching $H^P$ to the right order — a modified-Hamiltonian (backward-error) step plus homogeneity bookkeeping, none of which is given. Consequently 'This grants the existence of JHI's' is unsupported as written.

failure_location.quote: the induced family of diffeomorphisms $(\varphi_{L_s})_{s\in I}$ is a homogeneous Hamiltonian Poisson integrator of order $k$ for $H^P$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the missing contained argument: for a smooth near-identity family of homogeneous Poisson diffeomorphisms obtained from the approximate bisections, the generating time-dependent field is locally Hamiltonian (Poincare lemma) and 0-homogeneous, its local primitive can be chosen 1-homogeneous up to constants (constants not affecting flows), and standard perturbation of the order-$k$ variation-function approximation gives $\mathcal{H}_s=H^P+o(s^{k-1})$; also correct the misstatement of thm: ham flow.
issues.overall_effect: The existence of order-$k$ homogeneous Poisson Hamiltonian integrators and of Jacobi Hamiltonian integrators — the paper's main output — is claimed but not established by the source.
issues.title: Order-k integrator construction asserted without the needed modified-Hamiltonian argument
issues.why_classification: The main existence claim needs a contained but genuinely nontrivial lemma (local modified-Hamiltonian generation with homogeneity, plus order bookkeeping) absent from the source; with it all stated claims survive, so this is more than minor but not a loss of the result.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: since to preserving the Poisson structure and the Hamiltonian (up to a certain order), it preserves crucial properties of the geometry such as the symplectic foliation and Casimir functions.

issues.failure_explanation: The conclusion asserts exact preservation of the Hamiltonian. The paper's own definitions only guarantee that an integrator step is the exact flow of a modified Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}_s=H^J+o(s^{k-1})$, so $H^J$ is preserved only up to order $k$ — as the introduction itself correctly says '(up to a certain order)'. A JHI step generically changes the value of $H^J$, so the unqualified claim is false; the foliation and Casimir claims do follow since the maps are Jacobi diffeomorphisms.

failure_location.quote: This approach preserves not only the Jacobi structure and the Hamiltonian, but also the induced foliation and Casimir functions, which is particularly relevant in mechanical applications.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Qualify the claim: 'preserves the Jacobi structure, the induced foliation and the Casimir functions, and the Hamiltonian up to the order of the integrator'.
issues.overall_effect: The conclusion misstates the method's guarantee regarding the Hamiltonian.
issues.title: Conclusion claims exact Hamiltonian preservation
issues.why_classification: A one-phrase qualification ('up to order $k$') aligns the conclusion with the paper's definitions; nothing else is affected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We want to prove that $\pi_*(h_z^*(\alpha)) = h_z^*(\pi_*(\alpha)).$

issues.failure_explanation: The proof only shows that the fiber-integration operator $\pi_*$ commutes with the $\mathbb{R}^\times$-action. It never introduces the contraction of the star-shaped domain (the forms $\alpha$ it treats live on $U\times[0,1]$ with no stated relation to the forms on $U$ in the statement), never invokes the homotopy formula $dK+Kd=\mathrm{id}-s_0^*$ that produces the primitive, and never checks the equivariance of the contraction needed to conclude that the primitive is homogeneous. As written, the argument establishes an auxiliary fact and not the lemma's assertion of exactness with a homogeneous primitive.

failure_location.quote: then all $1$-homogeneous closed $p$-forms are exact and their primitive is also homogeneous.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Complete the standard proof: take $K=\pi_*\circ H^*$ with the equivariant contraction $H(x,t)=tx$, use the homotopy formula (with $s_0^*\alpha=0$ for $p\geq 1$) to obtain the primitive, and combine with the displayed $\pi_*$-compatibility to conclude it is homogeneous.
issues.overall_effect: The homogeneous Poincaré Lemma, announced as a key step for the normal-form theorems, is unproven as written (within thm:added-1's proof it is invoked only in the vacuous case of a point submanifold, which cannot occur for a free action, so no other labelled result is invalidated).
issues.title: Homogeneous Poincaré Lemma proof omits the contraction and homotopy formula
issues.why_classification: The missing steps are standard and contained; inserting the contraction and homotopy formula completes the proof without affecting anything else.
